docs.title: Sprinklr Webhooks: Architecture, Registration, and Use Cases
What are Webhooks?
docs.text: Webhooks are a combination of ‘web’ (HTTP-based communication) and the programming concept of ‘hooking’—allowing apps to intercept or respond to specific events. Webhooks let a source system notify a destination system in real time when an event occurs, by sending a HTTP request with relevant data (payload) to a registered endpoint.

docs.title: How to Register for a Webhook in Sprinklr
docs.text:
To register a webhook, the client provides:

  • Callback URL: The endpoint where event notifications (API calls with payloads) will be sent.

  • Authentication Type: For client-side verification of webhook source. Supported methods:

  • Public URL
  • Pre-shared key
  • Basic Auth

  • OAuth2.0

  • Subscription: Defines which change events the client wants to receive (e.g., case, message, comment, user updates). Conditional subscriptions are supported. For example:

  • Subscribe only when the case status changes—other case update events are filtered out.

  • Proxy Servers: Webhooks are sent via proxy servers. Clients can whitelist these server IPs.

docs.title: Sprinklr Webhook Backend Architecture
docs.text:
Sprinklr uses a robust architecture to process and deliver webhooks:

  1. Entity Update: The class com.spr.webhooks.dispatcher.client.WebhookDispatcherClientImpl processes updated entities (e.g., cases, messages, users).

  2. Each update is wrapped in a WebhookPacket and pushed to the Kafka queue: spr_webhook_event.

  3. Webhook Packet Handling: The class com.spr.webhooks.dispatcher.standalone.WebhookDispatcherStandaloneComponent handles incoming webhook packets.

  4. Retrieves relevant webhook subscription.
  5. Filters out entities that do not meet subscription conditions.

  6. Transforms valid packets into business objects—containing only client-relevant, non-secure data.

  7. Event Dispatching:

  8. The packet and subscription details are encapsulated into a WebhookEvent.

  9. Sent to another Kafka queue: webhook_event_queue.

  10. Webhook Delivery:

  11. The class com.spr.messageprocessor.listeners.webhook.WebhookEventListener receives the WebhookEvent.
  12. Depending on authentication type, sends the webhook to the registered callback URL.
  13. All delivery attempts (success/failure) are tracked in BigQuery.

docs.title: Usages of Sprinklr Webhooks
docs.text:
• Volume:

  • Handles ~288 million change events and 22 million webhook consumptions daily.

  • CRM Integration:

  • Integrates with systems like Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Zendesk, ServiceNow, etc.

  • Webhooks enable real-time synchronization of case, message, and profile data.

  • Digital Asset Management:

  • Integrates with Aprimo, Adobe Experience Manager (AEM), Bynder, and more.

  • Webhooks keep assets in sync with Sprinklr.

  • Bot Integrations:

  • Third-party bots use the Omnichannel Handover Protocol to receive real-time updates on case/message/conversation state transitions.

  • Editable Payloads:

  • Supports editable webhook payloads for self-serve partners.

docs.title: Why Use Webhooks?
docs.text: By triggering real-time updates for specific events, webhooks improve the efficiency and reliability of data exchange between systems. They are a key feature for enabling event-driven, integrated, and automated workflows.

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: You are given a list of logical circuit expressions. Each expression is written in prefix notation using only logical operators and constants. You must evaluate each expression and return its result as either 1 (logical true) or 0 (logical false).

docs.title: 🔣 Supported Symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning [ Start of expression block ] End of expression block & Logical AND | Logical OR ! Logical NOT 1 Logical TRUE 0 Logical FALSE

Each expression may be deeply nested and will follow correct prefix notation using the brackets [ and ] to group expressions.

docs.title: 🔁 Function Signature
docs.text: vector<int> circuitsOutput(vector<string> circuitsExpression);

docs.title: 📥 Input
docs.text:
• circuitsExpression: A list of strings, where each string is a valid circuit expression.
  • Each expression may contain up to 10^6 characters.

docs.title: 📤 Output
docs.text: • Return a list of integers where each value is either 1 or 0, representing the result of evaluating each expression.

docs.title: 🔒 Constraints
docs.text:
• 1 ≤ circuitsExpression.size() ≤ 10
  • Each expression is syntactically valid.
  • Only symbols: 0, 1, [, ], &, |, !, and commas (,) for separation.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: [1]

docs.title: ✅ C++ Solution
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int eval(queue<string> &q) {
    string t = q.front(); q.pop();
    if (t == "[") {
        string op = q.front(); q.pop();
        vector<int> args;
        while (q.front() != "]") {
            if (q.front() == "[") args.push_back(eval(q));
            else {
                string x = q.front(); q.pop();
                if (x == "!") {
                    int v = (q.front() == "[") ? eval(q) : (q.pop(), q.front() == "1");
                    if (q.front() != "[") q.pop();
                    args.push_back(!v);
                } else args.push_back(x == "1");
            }
        }
        q.pop(); // pop "]"
        if (op == "&") return all_of(args.begin(), args.end(), [](int x){ return x; });
        if (op == "|") return any_of(args.begin(), args.end(), [](int x){ return x; });
        if (op == "!") return !args[0];
    }
    return t == "1";
}

vector<int> circuitsOutput(vector<string> exprs) {
    vector<int> out;
    for (auto &s : exprs) {
        queue<string> q;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < s.size(); ++i) {
            if (isspace(s[i]) || s[i] == ',') continue;
            q.push(string(1, s[i]));
        }
        out.push_back(eval(q));
    }
    return out;
}

int main() {
    vector<string> expressions = {
        "[&, [&, 1, [!, 0]], [|, [|, 1, 0], [!, 1]]]"
    };
    vector<int> results = circuitsOutput(expressions);
    for (int res : results) cout << res << endl;  // Output: 1
}

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: Given an array of non-negative integers, perform a series of operations until the array becomes empty. The score is updated at each operation based on the sum of elements currently in the array. The goal is to maximize the overall score at the end.

docs.title: 🔢 Operations
docs.text:
• Operations are 1-indexed.
  • Odd-indexed operation: Add the sum of all integers in the array to the score.
  • Even-indexed operation: Subtract the sum of all integers in the array from the score.
  • After each operation, you must remove either the leftmost or rightmost element to continue.

Return the maximum score possible.

docs.title: 📥 Input
docs.text:
• An array of integers integerArray with size n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1000)
  • Each element is in range 0 ≤ integerArray[i] ≤ 10⁹

docs.title: 📤 Output
docs.text: • Return an integer: the maximum possible score

docs.title: 📘 Example
docs.text:
Input 

integerArray = [1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 6]

Output 

13

Explanation

  • Op 1 (odd): score += 18 → score = 18 → remove 6 → arr = [1,2,3,4,2]
  • Op 2 (even): score -= 12 → score = 6 → remove 2 → arr = [1,2,3,4]
  • Op 3 (odd): score += 10 → score = 16 → remove 4 → arr = [1,2,3]
  • Op 4 (even): score -= 6 → score = 10 → remove 1 → arr = [2,3]
  • Op 5 (odd): score += 5 → score = 15 → remove 3 → arr = [2]
  • Op 6 (even): score -= 2 → score = 13 → arr = []

docs.title: ✅ C++ Solution
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

long long dp[1001][1001][2];

long long solve(const vector<int>& arr, int l, int r, int opIndex) {
    if (l > r) return 0;
    int parity = opIndex % 2;
    if (dp[l][r][parity] != LLONG_MIN) return dp[l][r][parity];

    long long total = accumulate(arr.begin() + l, arr.begin() + r + 1, 0LL);
    long long gain = (parity == 1) ? total : -total;

    long long removeLeft = gain + solve(arr, l + 1, r, opIndex + 1);
    long long removeRight = gain + solve(arr, l, r - 1, opIndex + 1);

    return dp[l][r][parity] = max(removeLeft, removeRight);
}

long long getMaximumScore(vector<int> integerArray) {
    int n = integerArray.size();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; ++j)
            dp[i][j][0] = dp[i][j][1] = LLONG_MIN;

    return solve(integerArray, 0, n - 1, 1);
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 6};
    cout << getMaximumScore(arr) << endl; // Output: 13

    // Example with large numbers to test overflow handling
    vector<int> bigArr(1000, 1000000000);
    cout << getMaximumScore(bigArr) << endl; // Should not overflow
}

docs.title: 📝 Problem Description
docs.text:
When users are authenticated, they receive an authentication token. This token expires after a system-wide expiryLimit unless it is reset. If a reset request is made on or before the expiry time, the expiry is extended by expiryLimit minutes from the reset time.

  1. An unexpired token_id can be reset any number of times.
  2. A reset issued to a non-existent or an expired token_id is ignored.
  3. Once a token_id expires it cannot be reused.

Command syntax: [type, token_id, T] - Create command: Type 0 generates a token with id token_id at time T. Its expiry is set to T + expiryLimit. - Reset command: Type 1 resets the expiry to T + expiryLimit.

Perform a sequence of requests sorted ascending by their T parameter. Find the number of tokens that are active after all commands have been executed, at the maximum T of all requests.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
expiryLimit = 4
commands = [[0,1,1],[0,2,2],[1,1,5],[1,2,7]]

The maximum time T = 7. Only token_id = 1 is active at time 7. Return 1.

docs.title: ✅ C++ Solution
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int numberOfTokens(int expiryLimit, vector<vector<int>> commands) {
    unordered_map<int, int> expiry;
    int maxT = 0;
    for (auto &cmd : commands) {
        int type = cmd[0], token_id = cmd[1], T = cmd[2];
        maxT = max(maxT, T);
        if (type == 0) {
            expiry[token_id] = T + expiryLimit;
        } else if (type == 1) {
            if (expiry.count(token_id) && expiry[token_id] >= T)
                expiry[token_id] = T + expiryLimit;
        }
    }
    int active = 0;
    for (auto &[id, expT] : expiry) {
        if (expT > maxT) ++active;
    }
    return active;
}

int main() {
    int expiryLimit = 3;
    vector<vector<int>> commands = {{0,1,1}, {1,1,5}};
    cout << numberOfTokens(expiryLimit, commands) << endl; // Output: 0

    expiryLimit = 4;
    commands = {{0,1,1},{0,2,2},{1,1,5},{1,2,7}};
    cout << numberOfTokens(expiryLimit, commands) << endl; // Output: 1
}

docs.title: REST API: Medical Records by Weight
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Use the HTTP GET method to retrieve information from a database of patient medical records. Query https://jsonmock.hackerrank.com/api/medical_records to find all the records. The query result is paginated and can be further accessed by appending to the query string ?&page=num where num is the page number.

Each response contains a JSON with these fields: - page: current page - per_page: max results per page - total: total number of records in the search result - total_pages: total number of pages - data: array of JSON objects with medical records

Each record contains: - id: unique record id - timestamp: when record was generated (ms UTC) - userId: user id - userName, userDob - vitals: with fields like breathingRate - diagnosis: object with fields id, name, severity - doctor: object with fields id, name - meta: object with height and weight

docs.title: Fetch all medical records matching:
docs.text:
1. Records fetched should be diagnosed by the doctor with id doctorId and the diagnosis should belong to diagnosisId.
  2. For the users matching the first criteria:
  3. meta.weight should be greater than their personal average weight among the matched records
  4. vitals.breathingRate in the record should be greater than the given input breathingRate

If no records match, return [-1]. Otherwise, return a sorted array of ids.

docs.title: Java Solution (No Ambiguous JSONObject References)
docs.text:
import java.io.*;
import java.net.*;
import java.util.*;

public class Solution {
    public static int[] getRecordsDiagnosed(int doctorId, int breathingRate, int diagnosisId) throws Exception {
        List<org.json.JSONObject> allRecords = new ArrayList<>();
        int page = 1, totalPages = 1;
        while (page <= totalPages) {
            String url = "https://jsonmock.hackerrank.com/api/medical_records?page=" + page;
            HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) new URL(url).openConnection();
            conn.setRequestMethod("GET");
            BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(conn.getInputStream()));
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            String line;
            while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) sb.append(line);
            String jsonStr = sb.toString().trim();
            org.json.JSONObject obj = new org.json.JSONObject(jsonStr);
            totalPages = obj.getInt("total_pages");
            org.json.JSONArray data = obj.getJSONArray("data");
            for (int i = 0; i < data.length(); i++) allRecords.add(data.getJSONObject(i));
            page++;
        }

        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> userWeights = new HashMap<>();
        List<org.json.JSONObject> filtered = new ArrayList<>();
        for (org.json.JSONObject record : allRecords) {
            org.json.JSONObject diag = record.getJSONObject("diagnosis");
            org.json.JSONObject doc = record.getJSONObject("doctor");
            if (doc.getInt("id") == doctorId && diag.getInt("id") == diagnosisId) {
                filtered.add(record);
                int userId = record.getInt("userId");
                org.json.JSONObject meta = record.getJSONObject("meta");
                userWeights.putIfAbsent(userId, new ArrayList<>());
                userWeights.get(userId).add(meta.getInt("weight"));
            }
        }

        Map<Integer, Double> avgWeight = new HashMap<>();
        for (Map.Entry<Integer, List<Integer>> e : userWeights.entrySet()) {
            double sum = 0;
            for (int w : e.getValue()) sum += w;
            avgWeight.put(e.getKey(), sum / e.getValue().size());
        }

        List<Integer> answer = new ArrayList<>();
        for (org.json.JSONObject record : filtered) {
            int userId = record.getInt("userId");
            org.json.JSONObject meta = record.getJSONObject("meta");
            org.json.JSONObject vitals = record.getJSONObject("vitals");
            int weight = meta.getInt("weight");
            int br = vitals.getInt("breathingRate");
            if (weight > avgWeight.get(userId) && br > breathingRate) {
                answer.add(record.getInt("id"));
            }
        }

        if (answer.isEmpty()) return new int[]{-1};
        Collections.sort(answer);
        int[] arr = new int[answer.size()];
        for (int i = 0; i < answer.size(); i++) arr[i] = answer.get(i);
        return arr;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int doctorId = 3;
        int breathingRate = 20;
        int diagnosisId = 2;
        int[] result = getRecordsDiagnosed(doctorId, breathingRate, diagnosisId);
        for (int id : result) System.out.println(id);
    }
}

docs.title: Backend SDE-1 Project Ideas 🚀
docs.text: Here’s a curated list of backend projects perfect for SDE-1 level, with concise implementation details, tech stacks, and learning outcomes. Each project is designed to highlight core backend concepts like APIs, concurrency, authentication, and distributed systems.

docs.title: 1. 🌐 URL Shortener with Analytics
docs.text:
Overview: Build a service that converts long URLs into short, shareable links. Track every visit for analytics.

Core Features: - Generate unique short links (Base62/hash) - Redirect short links to original URLs - Track visits: IP, user-agent, timestamp - Analytics dashboard (clicks, devices, geo) - API endpoints for CRUD operations

Tech Stack: FastAPI / Flask, Redis, PostgreSQL

Learning Outcomes: - REST API design - Database schema for mapping and analytics - Caching with Redis - Security: rate limiting, input validation

Possible Extensions: - Custom aliases for short links - Expiry for links - QR code generation

docs.title: 2. 🔐 Auth-as-a-Service (JWT + OAuth2)
docs.text:
Overview: A plug-and-play authentication backend supporting email/password and OAuth2 (Google) login.

Core Features: - Register/login with email/password (bcrypt) - Google OAuth2 login - JWT access/refresh tokens - Token revocation (Redis) - Role-based access control (RBAC) - Middleware for protected routes

Tech Stack: Node.js / FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis

Learning Outcomes: - Secure password storage - OAuth2 flow - Stateless authentication with JWT - Session invalidation

Possible Extensions: - Email verification - Password reset - Multi-factor authentication

docs.title: 3. ⚙️ Job Queue System (Celery Lite)
docs.text:
Overview: A lightweight background job system to offload long-running tasks from the main app.

Core Features: - API to enqueue jobs - Redis-backed queue - Worker pool (multiprocessing/asyncio) - Track job status: pending, running, done, failed - Web dashboard for job monitoring

Tech Stack: Python, Redis, multiprocessing/asyncio

Learning Outcomes: - Producer-consumer pattern - Task serialization/deserialization - Worker orchestration - Real-time status updates

Possible Extensions: - Retry failed jobs - Scheduled jobs (cron) - Priority queues

docs.title: 4. 📁 File Upload & Streaming Service

Overview: A backend for uploading, storing, and streaming large files efficiently.

Core Features: - Chunked/resumable uploads - SHA-256 deduplication - Signed URLs for secure downloads - Media streaming with HTTP Range support - File metadata API

Tech Stack: Django/FastAPI, MinIO, Nginx

Learning Outcomes: - Handling large file uploads - Object storage integration - Secure file access - Streaming protocols

Possible Extensions: - Virus scanning - User quotas - Image/video thumbnail generation

docs.title: 5. 💬 Realtime Chat Backend
docs.text:
Overview: A scalable backend for real-time chat with user presence and message history.

Core Features: - WebSocket rooms with authentication - Redis pub-sub for horizontal scaling - Typing/read indicators - Offline message queue - Message history API

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text: Arrays are contiguous collections of elements, forming the basis for many algorithms and interview questions.

docs.title: 📖 Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Declaration & Initialization
  • Traversal (for, while, recursion)
  • Insertion & Deletion (at index, head, tail)
  • Slicing and Splicing
  • Searching (Linear, Binary Search)
  • Sorting (built-in, custom)
  • Prefix Sums
  • Sliding Window
  • Two Pointers
  • Hashing with Arrays
  • In-place Algorithms
  • Subarrays, Subsets, and Combinations

docs.title: 1. Sliding Window
docs.text:
• Find subarrays or substrings that match certain properties.
  • Problems: Maximum/Minimum subarray sum, longest substring without repeating characters.
int maxSumSubarray(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.size();
    int max_sum = 0, curr_sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) curr_sum += nums[i];
    max_sum = curr_sum;
    for (int i = k; i < n; ++i) {
        curr_sum += nums[i] - nums[i - k];
        max_sum = max(max_sum, curr_sum);
    }
    return max_sum;
}

docs.title: 2. Two Pointers
docs.text:
• Used for searching pairs/triplets, reversing, or partitioning.
  • Problems: Pair sum, move zeroes, reverse array in-place.
vector<int> twoSumSorted(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left = 0, right = nums.size() - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int s = nums[left] + nums[right];
        if (s == target) return {left, right};
        else if (s < target) ++left;
        else --right;
    }
    return {};
}

docs.title: 3. Prefix Sum
docs.text:
• Precompute cumulative sums to answer range queries in O(1).
  • Problems: Subarray sum equals k, range sum query.
vector<int> prefixSums(vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<int> ps(nums.size() + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.size(); ++i)
        ps[i + 1] = ps[i] + nums[i];
    return ps;
}

docs.title: 4. Hashing with Arrays
docs.text:
• Use hash maps (unordered_map/set) to count frequencies, detect duplicates, or map values.
  • Problems: Two sum, longest consecutive sequence.
bool hasDuplicate(vector<int>& nums) {
    unordered_set<int> seen;
    for (int n : nums) {
        if (seen.count(n)) return true;
        seen.insert(n);
    }
    return false;
}

docs.title: 5. Binary Search
docs.text:
• For searching in sorted arrays, or to answer "minimum/maximum" problems (search space).
  • Problems: Find element, first/last occurrence, search insert position.
int binarySearch(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left = 0, right = nums.size() - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
        else if (nums[mid] < target) left = mid + 1;
        else right = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

docs.title: 🧠 Tips & Tricks
docs.text:
• Know your STL algorithms: (e.g., std::accumulate, std::min_element, std::max_element)
  • Always check for empty arrays and edge cases (one element, all same, all zeros).
  • Think about space complexity: Can you do it in-place?
  • Know when to use O(n) vs O(n log n) approaches (prefix sum vs sorting).

docs.title: 📋 Array Template Functions
docs.text:
// Reverse in-place
void reverse(vector<int>& arr) {
    int left = 0, right = arr.size() - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        swap(arr[left], arr[right]);
        ++left;
        --right;
    }
}

// Rotate right by k
void rotate(vector<int>& arr, int k) {
    int n = arr.size();
    k = k % n;
    reverse(arr.begin(), arr.end());
    reverse(arr.begin(), arr.begin() + k);
    reverse(arr.begin() + k, arr.end());
}

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text: Graphs consist of nodes (vertices) and edges. They model relationships and connections between entities and are fundamental in computer science for representing networks, maps, and more.

docs.title: 📖 Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Directed and Undirected Graphs
  • Adjacency List and Matrix Representations
  • Traversals: BFS (Breadth-First Search), DFS (Depth-First Search)
  • Connected Components
  • Topological Sorting
  • Shortest Paths (Dijkstra, BFS for unweighted)
  • Cycle Detection
  • Minimum Spanning Tree (MST), Disjoint Set

docs.title: 1. Adjacency List Representation
docs.text:
// Graph as adjacency list
vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
// Add edge u-v (undirected)
adj[u].push_back(v);
adj[v].push_back(u);

docs.title: 2. Breadth-First Search (BFS)
docs.text:
void bfs(int start, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<bool>& visited) {
    queue<int> q;
    q.push(start);
    visited[start] = true;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int node = q.front(); q.pop();
        cout << node << " ";
        for (int neighbor : adj[node]) {
            if (!visited[neighbor]) {
                visited[neighbor] = true;
                q.push(neighbor);
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Depth-First Search (DFS)
docs.text:
void dfs(int node, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<bool>& visited) {
    visited[node] = true;
    cout << node << " ";
    for (int neighbor : adj[node]) {
        if (!visited[neighbor])
            dfs(neighbor, adj, visited);
    }
}

docs.title: 4. Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (DFS)
docs.text:
bool hasCycleUtil(int v, int parent, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<bool>& visited) {
    visited[v] = true;
    for (int nbr : adj[v]) {
        if (!visited[nbr]) {
            if (hasCycleUtil(nbr, v, adj, visited))
                return true;
        } else if (nbr != parent) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

bool hasCycle(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
    vector<bool> visited(n, false);
    for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) {
        if (!visited[v] && hasCycleUtil(v, -1, adj, visited))
            return true;
    }
    return false;
}

docs.title: 5. Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)
docs.text:
vector<int> topoSort(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
    vector<int> indegree(n, 0);
    for (auto& nbrs : adj)
        for (int v : nbrs)
            indegree[v]++;
    queue<int> q;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        if (indegree[i] == 0) q.push(i);
    vector<int> order;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop();
        order.push_back(u);
        for (int v : adj[u]) {
            if (--indegree[v] == 0)
                q.push(v);
        }
    }
    return order;
}

docs.title: 6. Shortest Path (Unweighted, BFS)
docs.text:
vector<int> shortestPath(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj, int start) {
    vector<int> dist(n, -1);
    queue<int> q;
    dist[start] = 0;
    q.push(start);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop();
        for (int v : adj[u]) {
            if (dist[v] == -1) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                q.push(v);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

docs.title: Linked Lists
docs.text: Linked lists are sequences of nodes, each pointing to the next. They are fundamental data structures for dynamic memory allocation and efficient insertions and deletions.

docs.title: 📖 Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Singly and Doubly Linked Lists
  • Insertion and Deletion Operations
  • Reversing a Linked List
  • Detecting Cycles (Floyd's Algorithm)
  • Merging and Splitting Lists
  • Finding the Middle Node
  • Removing N-th Node from End
  • Intersection and Union of Lists

docs.title: 1. Node Structure (C++ Template)
docs.text:
struct ListNode {
    int val;
    ListNode* next;
    ListNode(int x) : val(x), next(nullptr) {}
};

docs.title: 2. Reverse a Linked List (Iterative)
docs.text:
ListNode* reverse(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* prev = nullptr;
    while (head) {
        ListNode* nxt = head->next;
        head->next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}

docs.title: 3. Detect a Cycle (Floyd’s Tortoise and Hare)
docs.text:
bool hasCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

docs.title: 4. Find Middle Node
docs.text:
ListNode* findMiddle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
    }
    return slow;
}

docs.title: 5. Remove N-th Node From End
docs.text:
ListNode* removeNthFromEnd(ListNode* head, int n) {
    ListNode dummy(0);
    dummy.next = head;
    ListNode *first = &dummy, *second = &dummy;
    for (int i = 0; i < n + 1; ++i)
        first = first->next;
    while (first) {
        first = first->next;
        second = second->next;
    }
    second->next = second->next->next;
    return dummy.next;
}

docs.title: 6. Merge Two Sorted Lists
docs.text:
ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* l1, ListNode* l2) {
    ListNode dummy(0);
    ListNode* tail = &dummy;
    while (l1 && l2) {
        if (l1->val < l2->val) {
            tail->next = l1;
            l1 = l1->next;
        } else {
            tail->next = l2;
            l2 = l2->next;
        }
        tail = tail->next;
    }
    tail->next = l1 ? l1 : l2;
    return dummy.next;
}

docs.title: Trees
docs.text: Trees are hierarchical data structures with a root node and zero or more children per node. They are foundational for representing hierarchical data, enabling fast search, insert, and delete operations.

docs.title: 📖 Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Binary Tree, Binary Search Tree (BST), Heap
  • Tree Traversals: Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, Level-order (BFS)
  • Recursive and Iterative Approaches
  • Balanced vs. Unbalanced Trees
  • Common Patterns: DFS, BFS, Recursion

docs.title: 1. Node Structure (C++ Template)
docs.text:
struct TreeNode {
    int val;
    TreeNode* left;
    TreeNode* right;
    TreeNode(int x) : val(x), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}
};

docs.title: 2. Inorder Traversal (Recursive)
docs.text:
void inorder(TreeNode* root) {
    if (root) {
        inorder(root->left);
        cout << root->val << " ";
        inorder(root->right);
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Preorder Traversal (Recursive)
docs.text:
void preorder(TreeNode* root) {
    if (root) {
        cout << root->val << " ";
        preorder(root->left);
        preorder(root->right);
    }
}

docs.title: 4. Postorder Traversal (Recursive)
docs.text:
void postorder(TreeNode* root) {
    if (root) {
        postorder(root->left);
        postorder(root->right);
        cout << root->val << " ";
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Level-order Traversal (BFS)
docs.text:
void levelOrder(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    queue<TreeNode*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        TreeNode* curr = q.front();
        q.pop();
        cout << curr->val << " ";
        if (curr->left) q.push(curr->left);
        if (curr->right) q.push(curr->right);
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Insert into BST
docs.text:
TreeNode* insertBST(TreeNode* root, int val) {
    if (!root) return new TreeNode(val);
    if (val < root->val)
        root->left = insertBST(root->left, val);
    else
        root->right = insertBST(root->right, val);
    return root;
}

docs.title: 7. Search in BST
docs.text:
TreeNode* searchBST(TreeNode* root, int val) {
    if (!root || root->val == val) return root;
    if (val < root->val) return searchBST(root->left, val);
    else return searchBST(root->right, val);
}
